extracted.intended_audience: practitioners of early chemistry/alchemy, apothecaries, metallurgists, and artisans (readers of a natural-philosophy/chemical treatise)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for identifying, preparing, and using natural substances (amber, bitumen, salts, nitre, metals, pigments) and for metallurgical/pharmaceutical procedures in an early-modern alchemical treatise. Includes properties, extraction methods, safety warnings, and recipes for pigments and metal preparations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succinum (amber) physical behaviour and attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Succinum (amber) attracts light materials (chaff, straw, small twigs, leaves) and its attraction is influenced by humidity, heat, and friction; it is lighter than many stones and its behaviour differs from magnetism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that dry succinum, once heated or rubbed, draws in light matter; humid succinum contains oily juice and loses/changes its properties. Distinguishes succinum from magnetism (magnet attracts iron only; succinum's attraction varies and is enhanced by heat/friction). Notes tests: palea placed with succinum do not move when a magnet is interposed; succinum does not move a piece of straw when magnet is present, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types, colours, odour, and quality grades of amber
rubrics_metrics.description: Amber occurs in several kinds distinguished by colour, odour, and specific gravity (e.g., album — very light and fragrant; nigrum — heavy, without odour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists three genera (colour/odor/weight correspondences), notes that white/clear ambra is most fragrant and prized for perfumes and unguents; some varieties yield tears (lacryma) and are used medicinally/cosmetically. Advises selection of purer, less putrefied amber for making perfumes and unguents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amber's use to preserve small organisms and in unguents
rubrics_metrics.description: Amber (succinum) can enclose and preserve small creatures (flies, ants, fishlets) and is recommended as an ingredient in certain unguents and perfumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how creatures become trapped and preserved in the sticky amber; advises grinding the finest part into powder and adding to egg-yolk to make a fragrant ointment that attracts straw (i.e., to increase fragrance/viscosity). Recommends amber for cosmetic/medicinal ointments and notes that it resists putrefaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amber attraction enhanced by heat and friction
rubrics_metrics.description: The attractive property of succinum is increased by heat and rubbing; it becomes more active when purer parts of the stone are exposed or warmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that friction/heat free a purer part of the stone and increases attraction; compares to a cucurbit warmed with wax which acquires adhering property. Notes that when amber is rubbed with bitumina or mixed with ash it shows effects (agricola's observation that ash with amber will attract leaves when rubbed with iron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petroleum/oleum de Saxo — properties and medicinal use
rubrics_metrics.description: Petroleum (oleum de Saxo) is a thin, warm, heavily odorous oil derived from bitumen; traditionally used by kings and as a remedy for cold pains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Says it flows out by heat, is thin and warm, strongly smelling; people call it oleum de Saxo and use it for treating chronic cold maladies. Mentions it can be found in Palestine and affects vegetation near its springs (trees do not thrive where it flows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing asphalt/bitumen from sulphur and other combustibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Asphaltum/bitumen and sulphur differ in smell, burning duration, and effects; sulphur always smells ill and burns more readily, asphaltum may burn longer and is less volatile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns not to mistake asphaltum for other bituminous materials; notes that sulphur burns more readily and that asphaltum resists longer, so one should beware confusing types; mentions santhalut (a material) and different qualities (some used for particular purposes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sulphur's sensory and combustion characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sulphur has an always unpleasant odour and is more readily combustible than many bituminous substances; its natural occurrence and effects are contrasted with asphaltum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States sulphur is always foul-smelling, burns easily. In mixtures, sulphur aids ignition and persistence of fire; used to test and produce certain mineral transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation and extraction of halinitrum (salts) from soils and dung
rubrics_metrics.description: Halinitrum (saline efflorescences) forms in soils by exposure, animal excrement, and burning; one can cultivate and extract concentrated salts by layering soils/manures, leaching with water, evaporation, and repeated concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a procedure: collect perforated cists filled with bovine/equine/pigeon dung mixed with water; after staged fermentations and supernatant removal and re-evaporation, a concentrated halinitrum concretes; washed/evaporated material yields salt. Notes timescales (after five or six years certain soils yield more copiously) and the beneficial role of solar power and exposure cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nitrum (niter) occurrence and collection in caverns and sands
rubrics_metrics.description: Nitrum (saltpetre) commonly occurs as efflorescence in caves and certain sands (e.g., Nile sand); one may collect aqueous leachates and evaporate to obtain nitre; aphronitrum and other lighter efflorescences are related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes finding nitre in caverns where a leached white/loose part adheres to the rock (called aphronitrum), and processes of converting collected waters into nitre by concentration. Indicates geographical notes (Nile arena) and references to collectors (Albertus Magnus account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and uses of vitriol (vitriolum) and calchanti
rubrics_metrics.description: Vitriol (copper vitriol and similar sulfates) and calcined materials (calchanti) have strong fumes that can be detrimental to trees, but also produce intense colours and are used medicinally and artistically (inks, pigments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that fumes can damage vegetation and that vitriol smoke can blacken and harm organs. Notes vitriol's use in producing atrament (black ink), its smoky fumes, and its ability to produce vivid powders and colours upon calcination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of pyrites and metallic-origin minerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Pyritides and related fossil-metals differ from true metals: some are sterile (pyrites), others are metallic-bearing; their behaviour under heat distinguishes them and determines their suitability for various operations (e.g., producing glassy fumes, pigments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that some pyrites do not contain metal and are 'sterile' while others produce metallic residues; pyritides often yield spume and specific colours when roasted; used to make different types of mineral preparations (e.g., atrament, smaltum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cadmia, stibium, and lead family materials — sources and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Cadmia (zinc-related calamine/cadmia) and stibium (antimony/stibnite) are linked to lead and other metals; they occur in mines (e.g., Anzberg) and have characteristic colours useful for pigments or metalwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes cadmia often yields colours like saffron and suits certain alloys; discusses geographical sourcing and processing notes. Mentions that some metals are separable from ore by heat alone, others require special roasting or mixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chrysocholla, auripigmentum and other metallic pigments
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain earths and mineral products (chrysocholla, auripigmentum, cerulean-like earths) are produced from metals or their compounds and are valued pigments; their preparation and colour depend on the metal content and treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes that chrysocholla and azure-like pigments derive from metallic matrices; techniques include calcination and washing to produce bright colours; cautions that some substitutes sold commercially are inferior (e.g., substitutes for auripigmentum sold with sulphur to imitate colour). Advises selection of good material for durable colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argentum vivum (mercury) properties, amalgamation, and refining behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Argentum vivum (quicksilver/mercury) is a fluid metal that amalgamates with gold and silver, penetrates and dissolves metals, behaves like a dense liquid, and can be used to collect or separate precious metals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains methods: heating and placing gold in contact with mercury causes gold to be absorbed; different vessels (glass, leather) and temperatures influence amalgamation. Notes physical phenomena: mercury forms round droplets, resists wetting, and gathers into spheres; vegetation around mercury springs and freezing behaviour are observed and used to infer properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health hazards and precautions regarding mercury vapours
rubrics_metrics.description: Vapours from argentum vivum are hazardous: inhalation produces tremors, nervous dissolution, pulmonary disease, and other systemic effects; artisans handling sublimated mercury are at risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports observed cases of tremor and phthisis among workers; warns against daily inhalation and advises minimizing exposure in workspaces (avoid use near head/brain), prefer cooling and containment; notes protective measures like keeping mercury in wooden vessels and avoiding boiling that produces vapor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for sublimation, precipitation, and preparation of silver compounds/pigments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipes and stepwise methods are given for producing red precipitated silver, cinnabar-like pigments, and other silver-derived materials by mixing mercury/silver with vitriol, aceto, calcining, distillation in glass, repeated grinding and heating until desired colour/smoke appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example procedures: mix equal parts mercury and writing-ink (or 'atramentum') in a mortar with sharp vinegar until mercury seems to disappear; then bake in a glass vessel until it concretes; repeated distillation and heating in vitreous vessels until red smoke appears produces cinnabar-like pigment or precipitated silver. Detailed times, vessels (vitreum), and observations (red fumes, lack of vapor) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaltum and pforicum (glass/metal pigments) manufacture and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaltum (a vitreous blue pigment) and pforicum are produced by combining calcined (calchanto) and vitreous materials with metallic spumes and roasting until colours develop; the resulting smaltum is used to fill gilded cavities and for decorative colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives recipe: mix parts of calchanto, alumen, and glassy stone, roast with new pots and charcoal until reddened; smaltum accepts many varied colours and is used opulently for ornament. Also describes extraction of 'recrementum' (the metal-retaining foam) during smelting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of processed silver/metal compounds in medicine and cosmetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooked/processed silver (e.g., 'argentum coctum' or precipitated silver) is used in lotions, cosmetics (to enhance the complexion), and some medicines; effects include brightening the face though it may cause oral fetor or tooth issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States women use cooked silver for beauty; also used in medicines against putrefactions and ulcers. Warns of side effects (bad breath) and that some preparations alter the voice or mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour of metals in fire and the role of oil/moisture in refining
rubrics_metrics.description: The combustible or refractory behaviour of a metal in fire depends on its dryness and oiliness; adding lead or other substances influences melting, liquefaction, and separation. Humid or oily metals produce fumes and change during heating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that adding lead causes alloys to melt differently; dry metals resist melting and some perish less quickly in fire. Observes that organic oils and greases affect fusion and brittleness (cold makes metals fragile). Advises choice of fluxes/adjuncts (like vitriol, sulfur, oil) based on desired outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and selection of mineral matrices and lapis for metal extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals are often found in a matrix; selecting the appropriate matrix (lapis cum matrice) and distinguishing true metal-rich stone from mere colored earth is crucial for successful metallurgical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that many better metals lie within lapidous matrices and that some earths (galena, ochre, etc.) are more fit for liquation. Recommends examining the ore's appearance, density and reaction to heat to judge value.
